name: Fallingwater
label: Fallingwater
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/354728127: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fallingwater' (44 m across).
notes: Frank Lloyd Wright's famous house built over the Bear Run waterfall.

text.description: Fallingwater is a house museum in the Laurel Highlands of southwestern Pennsylvania, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright as a weekend retreat for Edgar J. Kaufmann Sr. and his wife Liliane. It is built partly over a waterfall on the Bear Run stream. Its long concrete terraces are cantilevered, reaching out from a chimney with no support at the far end. That gives you strong horizontal lines to set against the rock, the trees and the moving water. The house is made of locally quarried stone, reinforced concrete, steel and plate glass, so the textures also reward a closer look. The Kaufmanns began using the house in 1937, and the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy has run it as a visitor attraction since 1963. It is a National Historic Landmark and part of a World Heritage Site. The house sits under a canopy of forest and is not on a prominent hilltop, so expect dappled light and a lot of green around it. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north-west of the subject. That is close enough to fit the main block in one frame with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), and to pick out terraces and stonework with the zoom. Take a wide shot first, then a few tighter ones. The stream can freeze in winter and dry up in summer, so the waterfall will not always look the same.
text.geographic_location: Fallingwater stands in Stewart Township, Fayette County, above the Bear Run stream, between the communities of Ohiopyle and Mill Run.
text.directions_text: Fallingwater is near Pennsylvania Route 381, between Ohiopyle and Mill Run, about 72 miles (116 km) south-east of Pittsburgh. The visitor pavilion is the starting point on site; follow the paths from there towards the house. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole house and its terraces from this close. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the stonework, the glass and the edges of the terraces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Take a few steps to either side if trees block part of the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the long terrace edges with them so the horizontal lines stay level. Keep a little of the surrounding trees and rock in the frame to show how the house sits in the landscape. Try one wide shot and one tighter shot of the terraces. Hold your phone steady against a rail or tree if one is nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky and water do not wash out. If the light is patchy, take two or three shots and keep the best. A Live Photo can catch moving leaves or water. Use panorama only if you can move slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light on an overcast day suits the stonework and green canopy, with less harsh dappled shadow. Whenever you go, check the official site for visiting times before you set out.

text.access_note: Fallingwater is a ticketed house museum run as a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go for tours, entry and which areas of the grounds you can visit.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point, on the north-west side of the house, the house is seen from a side that is not the classic downstream view over the falls.
Overcast light gives softer, more even results than bright sun under the forest canopy.
Live Photos can capture the movement of leaves and water.
There is a rail or tree near the stand-here point that can be used to steady the phone.

photo.from: Own photo, taken 3 m from the phone icon

name: Kentuck Knob
label: Kentuck Knob
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kentuck Knob Overlook' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Kentuck Knob' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/428811366: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kentuck Knob' (46 m across).
notes: Hilltop Usonian house by Frank Lloyd Wright near Ohiopyle.

text.description:
Kentuck Knob is a small house designed by Frank Lloyd Wright for I. N. Hagan, an ice-cream company owner, and his wife Bernardine. It was completed in 1956 and sits on the southern slope of a wooded knoll. The walls are locally quarried stone and redwood, with a broad overhanging copper roof, and the plan is built around a hexagon. It is a National Historic Landmark. The house is a few miles from Fallingwater, and the Hagans first heard of Wright through the family who built Fallingwater.

It photographs well because the low roofline and the stone seem to grow out of the hillside. The best exterior view is usually from the back. From the informal overlook on the east side of the house, about 100 m south-east of it, you see the sandstone walls and the cantilevered roof, with the Youghiogheny River gorge and Laurel Highlands ridges behind. Trees can screen the gorge itself, so expect the ridges and treetops to do most of the work in the background. The entrance side, with the carport and the roofline set into the hill, is a good second shot. So is a side view from higher up the hillside, framed by trees.

No photography is allowed inside the house, so plan on outdoor pictures only.
text.geographic_location: Kentuck Knob is in Stewart Township, Fayette County, Pennsylvania, a few miles from Fallingwater rather than in the town itself. The house stands on the southern slope of a wooded knoll above the Youghiogheny River gorge.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport stop nearby. The house is reached by road, along a long gravel driveway from Pennsylvania Route 2010, which runs through woods. Fallingwater is about a 7-mile drive to the northeast of Kentuck Knob, so from Fallingwater head south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the house and ridges together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the roof gets cut off. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the stone and the copper roof edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kentuck Knob Overlook (a few steps from the back terrace, on the east side of the house). The house's rear side with its sandstone walls and cantilevered roof, with the Youghiogheny River gorge and Laurel Highlands ridges behind it. From here the house lies to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the roofline along the upper third, with the ridges above it. Keep the horizon level, since the long horizontal roof shows any tilt. For a different view, try the entrance side with the carport, or a side view from the hillside framed by trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky and ridges keep some colour. If the roof overhang makes the walls too dark, tap the shaded wall and raise the exposure slightly. Try a panorama only if you can keep the phone steady and level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light on a bright overcast day suits the stone and the copper roof, because it avoids hard shadows under the overhang. Autumn leaf colour could add warmth to the trees around the house.

text.access_note: The house is open to the public for tours, and it is not clear whether the overlook or hillside areas can be used without a tour ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ohiopyle State Park
label: Ohiopyle State Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ohiopyle Falls Observation Deck' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ohiopyle Falls Observation Deck' (way/606721771): middle (29 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/12915608: large area 'Ohiopyle State Park' (21666 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Park around the Youghiogheny River gorge with the Ohiopyle waterfalls and rapids.

text.description: Ohiopyle State Park covers about 20,500 acres of forested gorge country in Fayette County, Pennsylvania, and Ohiopyle Falls is its best-known sight. The falls are only about 20 feet (6 m) high, but they stretch right across the Youghiogheny River, so the picture is all about width and moving white water. The name comes from a Lenape phrase meaning 'it turns very white', which suits the frothy water. Guides call this the most photographed spot in the park. From the Ohiopyle Falls Observation Deck you look across the full width of the falls, with the tree-covered Ferncliff Peninsula behind. The deck is beside the parking lot on Main Street (Route 381), so it is the easiest viewpoint to reach. The park opened to the public in 1965 and was formally dedicated in 1971. It sits on the site of old railway-age resorts that drew visitors to the falls. For a different angle, Baughman Rock Overlook gives long views down the river gorge, and the Ohiopyle High Bridge looks down on the rapids through its arches. Kayakers sometimes run the rapids below. Take a few wide shots first, then move in for details of the water. The falls area was reported as being rebuilt, so check current construction and parking before you go.
text.geographic_location: This spot is in the village of Ohiopyle, in the Falls Day Use Area at the centre of Ohiopyle State Park, beside the parking lot on Main Street (Route 381). It is several miles from the Fallingwater house itself.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. Start from the village of Ohiopyle and head for the parking lot on Main Street (Route 381). The observation decks are right beside that parking lot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole width of the falls and the forest behind. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the white water or the trees of Ferncliff Peninsula.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (observation decks beside the parking lot on Main Street / Route 381). The full width of Ohiopyle Falls spanning the Youghiogheny River, with the forested Ferncliff Peninsula behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the lip of the falls along a lower line, so the water fills the frame and the trees sit above it. Try one wide shot and one tighter zoomed shot. If you have time, Baughman Rock Overlook is a good second viewpoint for long gorge views.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest white water to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the foam keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the water. Wipe your lens first, as spray may smear it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there is less glare on the water.

text.access_note: The falls area is part of a state park with public viewing decks; check the official site before you go for current access, construction and parking.
claims_not_in_sources: Very bright white water can look overexposed on a phone, so lowering the exposure slider usually helps.
Spray from the falls may get on a phone lens, so it helps to wipe it first.

name: Ohiopyle High Bridge
label: Ohiopyle High Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ferncliff Trail' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ferncliff Trail' (way/158604737): edge nearest the subject (1179 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9883943: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ohiopyle High Bridge' (211 m across).
notes: Railroad bridge, now trail bridge, high above the Youghiogheny River.

text.description:
The Ohiopyle High Bridge is a long steel bridge that carries the Great Allegheny Passage trail across the Youghiogheny River just north of Ohiopyle. It opened in 1912 as part of the Western Maryland Railway's push from Cumberland, Maryland, to Connellsville, Pennsylvania, the last major railroad built in Pennsylvania. It stands more than 100 feet higher than the nearby Ohiopyle Low Bridge. The railway lost its importance in the later 20th century, and the bridge was rehabilitated and reopened for public use in 1989.

This spot is on the Ferncliff Trail, where you look up at the bridge from below. From here the high deck stretches across the gorge, with the river beneath it and trees around it, including autumn colour. Guides describe the bridge as striking from below as well as from above. The Ferncliff Trail reaches the bridge's lower side as the last highlight before the trailhead, so it makes a good finish to a walk.

From the deck you get a different picture: the Youghiogheny gorge, the rapids below and the Laurel Highlands behind, though the bridge itself only appears if you include the rail. A named scenic view area nearby is another option; check its position on the map. Take your time on the trail, keep your phone strapped or held firmly near the edge of the water, and look for a gap in the trees that frames the deck.
text.geographic_location: The bridge is just north of Ohiopyle village, crossing the Youghiogheny River in the gorge. Ohiopyle is about 10 miles from Fallingwater (Mill Run).
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed nearby, so the spot is reached on foot from Ohiopyle village. One guide describes a walk of about 0.4 miles north-west from Sheridan and Sherman Streets in Ohiopyle to the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole deck, the gorge and the trees into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view of the span. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the steel structure high above.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Ferncliff Trail (on the Ferncliff Peninsula trail, looking up at the bridge from below). The high steel deck of the bridge seen from underneath, framed by the gorge, river and autumn trees. The high steel deck should sit in the upper part of the frame, with the gorge, river and trees below and around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the deck along the upper third line, with trees or the river making a natural frame. Keep the phone level so the bridge does not lean. If you want a different view, the deck itself looks out over the river and rapids, but then the bridge is only in the picture if you include the rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the underside of the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the steel. Panorama can work for a wide sweep of the gorge if you hold the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Autumn foliage appears in the view of the bridge from the Ferncliff Trail, so the trees may add colour in that season. Gentler light earlier or later in the day usually suits a bridge against the sky better than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The bridge is part of the Great Allegheny Passage rail trail and the Ferncliff Trail can flood in high water, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bear Run
label: Bear Run
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Overlook' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Paradise Overlook' (node/6363819388): point.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: The stream and trail with the classic downstream view of Fallingwater.

text.description:
Fallingwater stands on Bear Run, at the locality known as Mill Run, and the Overlook on the grounds loop path is where most visitors take their photo of the house. From here you look across the water to the house's stacked, cantilevered terraces, which sit above the Bear Run falls, with the stream in the foreground. It is the classic postcard view, and it works well on a phone because the whole scene fits in one frame.

The stream itself is about 5 miles (8 km) long and runs into the Youghiogheny River in Fayette County, Pennsylvania. It lies inside the Bear Run Nature Reserve, which is looked after by the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy, and it is a designated Pennsylvania Scenic River. The surrounding valley is about 89% forest, which is why the greenery fills the frame in almost every shot.

For your photo, use the Overlook as your viewpoint and let the water run along the bottom of the picture, with the house sitting above it. If you want a change of scene, Paradise Overlook gives a wider view over the wooded valley and the house, with the stream lower down. Bird's Eye View looks down on the house and trees, but you cannot see the waterfall from there. The lower view beside the stream, reached by the bridge near the house, tends to be crowded. The paths can be muddy after rain, so wear shoes with a decent grip.
text.geographic_location: On the grounds of Fallingwater, on the grounds loop path at the Overlook, across Bear Run from the house. The stream flows right below the house, at the locality known as Mill Run.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is given for this spot. The nearest town is Ohiopyle, a few miles from Fallingwater on PA State Route 381. Once you are inside the grounds, follow the grounds loop path and look for the Overlook as marked on the grounds map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the house, the falls and the stream in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more of the foreground water and trees, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the terraces.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Overlook (on the grounds loop path, across Bear Run from the house). The classic postcard view of the house's cantilevered terraces above the Bear Run falls, with the stream in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the falls on the lower third, with the terraces along the middle line. Keep the phone level so the house's straight lines stay straight. For an alternative, Paradise Overlook gives a wider view of the valley with the stream lower in the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the house to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright water and sky do not wash out. Try a Live Photo and pick the frame you like best, as the moving water can look different in each one. Wipe the lens before you shoot, since spray and damp air can smear it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a soft, overcast day or when the sun is not shining directly onto the water, and try to arrive early or late to avoid the crowds. After rain the stream looks fuller, but the paths are muddier.

text.access_note: The grounds need a paid grounds pass, and winter access may be limited, so check the official site before you go.
